extracted.intended_audience: LaTeX users / mathematicians who want to typeset graphs and commutative diagrams (e.g., category theory)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for producing graphs and commutative diagrams in LaTeX using the Xy-pic package: installation, choosing an environment, node/arrow syntax, label placement, positioning, and stylistic variants (dashed/curved arrows, multiple arrows, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include Xy-pic package in preamble
rubrics_metrics.description: For the time being, I want to show off just the basics of the Xy-pic package ... We start by making sure that we have the commmand \usepackage[all]{xy} in the LaTeX document preamble.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always include \usepackage[all]{xy} in the document preamble before using \begin{xy} or \xymatrix. The '[all]' option enables the commonly used features; omit or change options only if you know the consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose between \begin{xy} and \xymatrix
rubrics_metrics.description: One is the environment \begin{xy}...\end{xy} and the other is \xymatrix{....}. The latter is simpler to use, but is not setup to make complicated diagrams, which the former is (at least this was BingChat's summation of their basic differences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use \xymatrix for simple, grid-like commutative diagrams; use the full \begin{xy} environment for more complicated layouts, fine control of node placement, curved arrows, and advanced styling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Node placement and naming using coordinates
rubrics_metrics.description: Nodes are placed with coordinate syntax such as (0,20)*+{A}="a"; (20,20)*+{B}="b"; ... which creates a node at the given coordinates and assigns it a name for later reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use (x,y)*+{<content>}="name" to put arbitrary content (including math) at precise coordinates and give the node a label name (in quotes) for arrow references. This allows explicit positioning rather than relying on matrix layout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic arrow command syntax
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrows between nodes use the \ar command, e.g. {\ar "a";"b"}; or {\ar (30,50)*+{V}; (60,0)*+{Y}}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference nodes by their names in quotes or by coordinate expressions. The semicolon separates source and target. You can place \ar commands on separate lines; use % at line endings to avoid unwanted spaces/newlines in LaTeX source when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrow label placement via ?*!/_ or ?*!/^
rubrics_metrics.description: The letter that is placed above/below the arrow in the diagram, or to the left or right of the arrow is controlled by the options of '_' or '^' that follows the '?*!/' string. If you try it one way and that doesn't work, do it the other way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use syntax like ?*!/_2mm/{\alpha} or ?*!/^2mm/{U} to attach labels to arrows and to offset them by a numeric amount (e.g. 2mm). Try both '_' (below/left) and '^' (above/right) if label position isn't as expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjusting label offset (numeric offset in ?*!/...)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples use ?*!/_2mm/{\alpha} and ?*!/^2mm/{f} showing numeric offset in the label placement command.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a numeric offset (e.g. 2mm) after '_' or '^' inside the ?*!/ modifier to fine-tune how far the label sits from the arrow. Vary the sign and magnitude to avoid collisions with arrowheads or other diagram elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrow styles: dashed, dotted, and other modifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: You can draw different arrow styles using syntax like {\ar@{-->} "a";"d"}; and {\ar@{--} (30,50)*+{V}; (30,20)*+{U}}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use @{...} after \ar to change arrow style (dashed, dotted, harpoons, etc.). Combine style modifiers with curved-arc modifiers and label placement to represent different semantic relationships (e.g., a dashed arrow to indicate a different kind of morphism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Curved arrows via @/^.pc/ or @/_.pc/ modifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Curved arrows are made with constructs like {\ar@/^.75pc/(30,0)*+{B}; (65,0)*+{C}}% and {\ar@/_.75pc/(0,0)*+{A}; (40,0)*+{B}}%
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use @/^.Xpc/ or @/_.Xpc/ to create arcs curving above (^.) or below (_.) the straight line; adjust the numeric value (e.g. .75pc) to control curvature. Useful for drawing parallel arrows between the same nodes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depicting epimorphisms, monomorphisms, and product diagrams
rubrics_metrics.description: The page shows example diagrams titled 'Epimorphism', 'Monomorphism', 'Cartesian Product One', 'Cartesian Product Two' demonstrating how to assemble multiple arrows, curved arrows, dashed arrows, and projection labels (e.g., \pi_x, \pi_y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the examples to represent common categorical constructions: combine curved double arrows and labels for epi/mono conventions, use projection arrows with labels \pi_x, \pi_y to show product diagrams, and use dashed vs solid arrows to indicate hypothetical or special maps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positioning diagrams horizontally with \hbox and \hskip
rubrics_metrics.description: So, why did I put the xy diagram into an hbox? I did that so that I could control the horizontal placement of the diagram ... The command \hskip1.6in shoves the hbox and its contents 1.6 inches to the right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wrap a diagram in an \hbox{...} and use \hskip<length> to shift it horizontally when finer placement is needed. The author notes that there may be more elegant methods, but this is a simple TeX-era technique that works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comment out lines rather than delete them
rubrics_metrics.description: Notice that I have commented out the lines of code I didn't want to use in this diagram, but might want to activate in a later version of the diagram. In LaTeX, sometimes it's more efficient to comment out a line or lines of code rather than the delete them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use % to comment out example or optional \ar or node lines in your source so you can re-enable them later. This preserves alternate layout attempts and makes iterative editing easier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nodes may contain arbitrary math and macros
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples include nodes containing math constructions such as \ket{\psi} \ket{0} and expressions like \alpha\ket{00} + \beta\thin \ket{10}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can place complex mathematical content and LaTeX macros inside node braces { ... } — Xy-pic will render rich math content within nodes. Be mindful of spacing and use \thin or similar spacing commands if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple arrows between the same nodes and duplicate labels
rubrics_metrics.description: The examples show both a dashed and a solid arrow from one node to another and also two arrows from the same source to target each labeled (e.g., {\ar@{-->} "b";"d"}?*!/_2mm/{\varphi}; {\ar "b";"d"};?*!/_2mm/{\varphi};).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may draw several arrows between the same nodes (solid + dashed, multiple curved arcs) and assign labels to each. Use curvature and offsets to avoid overlapping arrows and labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syntax details: semicolons, percent signs, and quoting names
rubrics_metrics.description: Code examples use semicolons to separate source and target in \ar, percent signs (%) at ends of lines in code, and quoted node names like "a","b" for references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminate coordinate/node specs and arrow commands appropriately; use % to avoid spurious whitespace or to comment out lines; enclose node names in quotes when referencing them in \ar commands. Pay attention to TeX spacing rules when mixing Xy-pic with surrounding text.
